title: Chapter 1
author: Rob Xie

paragraphs.text: The crawl at the bottom of the screen said BREAKING, which in the taxonomy of modern cable news meant anything from a nuclear detonation to a celebrity's new haircut. Adrian Marsh reached for his coffee, already cold, and watched the helicopter footage circle a glass tower in San Francisco's South of Market district like a vulture that had spotted something interesting.

paragraphs.text: "Corporate espionage," the anchor said, her voice carrying the practiced urgency of someone who delivered catastrophe with the same cadence as weather reports. "Federal agents have arrested a suspect in what authorities are calling one of the most sophisticated breaches of a major technology company in recent years."

paragraphs.text: Adrian set the mug down. It was Monday evening. He was in his living room in Berkeley, in the craftsman bungalow he'd bought with his early-stage equity — the modest payout from rounds one and two, before the real money arrived for the people who stayed. The house was modest. His colleagues in the Computer Science department found it suspiciously so for a man who had been present at the founding of a company whose worth now dwarfed some fairly successful countries. What they didn't understand was the difference between being present at the founding and being present at the payday. Adrian had been pushed out long before the paydays came.

paragraphs.text: It had happened gradually — it always did. First the board expanded. Then the "growth advisors" arrived, men in expensive shoes who spoke about users as "addressable markets" and ethics as "brand risk." Adrian fought back. He argued for constraints on the behavioral prediction models, for transparency reports, for opt-out mechanisms that would have cost the company a fraction of its advertising revenue. He was told he was out of touch. He was told the market wouldn't wait. He was told, in a particularly memorable board meeting, that his concerns were "academically interesting but commercially irrelevant." His influence shrank with each funding round, each new executive hire, each quarterly report that proved the money people right and the ethics people expendable. By the end, he wasn't fired. He was simply no longer invited to the meetings that mattered.

paragraphs.text: He took the gracious exit. Cashed out his early equity — enough to be comfortable, nothing close to what the later rounds generated. Some nights, alone in the kitchen with nothing but the hum of the refrigerator, he let himself calculate what those later stakes would be worth today. The number was grotesque. The anguish was not that he had walked away on principle. The anguish was that he had been pushed out before he'd even had that chance. He'd given most of the proceeds away. Kept the house, the books, and a quiet, persistent guilt that no amount of philanthropic tax deductions could extinguish.

paragraphs.text: On screen, the footage cut to a perp walk. A young man, mid-twenties, East Asian, slight build, the kind of person you'd picture leaving a university lab after hours, still wearing his badge. He was being escorted from the building in handcuffs. And he was smiling. Not broadly, not triumphantly, but with a faint, unsettling curl at the corners of his mouth, as though he had finished something important and the handcuffs were merely an administrative detail. That expression bothered Adrian more than terror would have. Terror he could have understood. This was something else.

paragraphs.text: NovaMind. He knew NovaMind. Everyone in his field knew NovaMind. They were one of the companies building what the industry euphemistically called "foundation models," artificial intelligence systems so large and so general-purpose that they functioned less like software and more like infrastructure. The electrical grid of the cognitive age. NovaMind's specialty was behavioral prediction: feed the model enough data about a person's digital footprint and it could forecast their decisions with an accuracy that made free will feel like a construct to put our minds at ease.

paragraphs.text: Adrian had written about this. He had, in fact, written compulsively about this — as if the writing could retroactively justify the years of fighting a tide he was never going to turn. He'd watched the generation of entrepreneurs who replaced him and saw a class corrupted beyond recovery, drunk on the power these systems gave them, blind to what that power was doing. He couldn't change them. He'd tried, and they'd shown him the door with a severance package and a polite suggestion that he "pursue his passion for education."

paragraphs.text: So he did. The next generation, the students filing into his seminars each fall with their laptops and their earnestness — they still had a chance. Teaching was his way of fighting back. It was the one lever he believed he could still pull. Three peer-reviewed papers, a book chapter, and an op-ed in The Atlantic that his department chair had called career-limiting. His argument was straightforward: systems like NovaMind's didn't just predict behavior — they created the conditions for moulding it. People became clay. The algorithms shaped them in whichever direction their operators desired, subtly, persistently, and without any form of detection. When you can model a population's decision-making at scale, the distance between prediction and manipulation is measured in one board meeting.
